toc.title: You notice the effects, not neuroception itself
The practice: one sense, on purpose

blocks.p: You learned the Polyvagal Theory. Now what? How do you apply this knowledge to your everyday life? This tip focuses on understanding and identifying neuroception. Neuroception is commonly misunderstood, so we need to spend some time first on clearly understanding what it is. Then we'll apply the idea to your life in a very easy, practical, and approachable way.
We need to understand neuroception top down to then recognize it bottom up. I'll build the definition in steps, starting in the simplest but most accurate terms I can muster.
Step one. Neuroception is your body's way of detecting safety or danger. Super simple definition, but it's of course more complex.

Step two. Neuroception is your body's way of detecting safety or danger or life threat. When you neurocept safety, your body accesses its ventral vagal safety state. When you neurocept danger, your body turns off the safety activation, resulting in increased sympathetic flight or fight activation. And if it detects a life threat, then the dorsal vagal shutdown system kicks in. That's a very one-dimensional, cartoony way of putting things, but we're starting off simple.

Step three. Neuroception is your body's way of detecting safety or danger or life threat before your conscious mind is aware of these things. Neuroception is not a conscious process. You're not aware of it while it's happening. You're only aware of it after it's happened. You notice the effects of neuroception, not neuroception itself.

Step four. Neuroception is your body's way of detecting safety or danger or life threat from the internal or external world before your conscious mind is aware of these things. Neuroception responds to more than the external world, like the loud boom of thunder above. It also responds to the internal world, like if you're chronically ill.

Neuroception is not conscious thought. It's not consciously directed. It's a biological process happening in the brainstem. The brainstem is where top-down and bottom-up communication meet. Your body sends signals of safety or danger up to the brainstem, and your higher brain structures send signals of safety or danger down to the brainstem. The body and brain meet and discuss safety and danger at the brainstem.
Dr. Porges put the limits of that top-down side plainly when he was on the podcast:

q: What higher brain structures can do are in part limited by the state that the brainstem is in.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [Dr Stephen Porges Interview: Mental Disorders, Substance Use, Psychiatry & the Polyvagal Theory (episode 15)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/a3c6a54a-11a7-4f2f-9d74-db287c774d08)

blocks.p: Let's use a metaphor. It's silly, but hopefully more understandable. Think of your body and the rest of your brain as people, and your brainstem is a person too. So we have three people. The brainstem is the decision maker of the group. The brain and the body come to the decision maker and give it their data.
The brain says, "This person whose thoughts I have, they're a real idiot. They're going to get fired soon. And everyone in the office talks about them behind their back."

The brainstem says, "That's not good. Sounds like danger. So we'll keep things on high alert. Brain, I need you to focus intently on maybe getting fired and how maybe nobody likes this person. All of your energy needs to go to focusing on these dangers."
The brain says, "But we have a thing on Saturday, and I need to get the kids to the doctor."
And the brainstem says, "Nope. Just focus on the most immediate danger. All systems need to prioritize these dangers."
Meanwhile, the body is there too, and has a message for the decision maker: "Things are pretty tense down here. I'm super tight in the gut area, and I can't get enough air into my chest."

So the brainstem says, "OMG. Things are worse than I thought. Sounds like a ton of dangers. Okay, body, let's also stay on high alert. Keep tense, keep ready. Focus all energies on maintaining hypervigilant readiness. If there's anything off, let me know immediately. If somebody at work has a slightly tense voice, prioritize that. I'll let the brain know, and it'll put a response into action."
And things can stay this way. Not indefinitely, exactly. But if you're in a traumatized state, that defensiveness is chronic, and potentially indefinite if nothing else changes.

The good news is that the body is also sending other signals to the brainstem, like the smell of food on the way to work, or the sight of pink cherry blossoms on a tree outside a window. And the brain can remember moments of connection. These messages go to the brainstem decision maker too.
The point is that the brainstem is where all the polyvagal state shifting takes place, and it shifts based on the cues it receives from the body and the rest of the brain.
Let's create a fictional scenario to bring this to life a little more.

It's Sarah's first week at her new job, and she's attending a team meeting. She arrives a few minutes before it starts, wanting to make a good impression on her colleagues and the higher-ups. She says to herself, "You got this, Sarah."

She opens the door to the conference room and lifts her leg to take a step in. Before her foot can land, her eyes take in the harsh brightness of the fluorescent bulbs above. Her ears take in the dull hum and the chatter of her colleagues. Her nose picks up the slight scent of disinfectant. Her eyes take in the view of the city from the 50th floor, and the backs of her colleagues' heads, facing away from her. A subtle tension grips her shoulders, and her breathing becomes more shallow, up into her chest.

Her foot finally falls for that first step into the room. The second foot follows, and her legs tense as she stands stoically still like a statue, her eyes widening to scan the room. A thought pierces her mind like a lightning bolt: "This is too much for me. I am not ready for this. And they all know."

Is Sarah neurocepting danger? Obviously. She enters a freeze state based on what she's picking up in the room. The onset of the freeze is rapid, and she has no idea why. To her, it's imposter syndrome. That's what she would say to herself. She thinks people are judging her. But really, she entered the room with some anxiety already, and then the room itself and the people in it gave her brainstem numerous tiny sensory danger cues: the height of the room overlooking the city, the lighting, the voices, the faces of her colleagues, and the scent in the room.

These things aren't dangerous, but they cue danger in her body. She's unaware of all of these sensory pieces at a conscious level, but her brainstem picked up on every single one of them and shifted her body into a life threat state. That's what the freeze was.
Let's take the story a step further.

Sarah is standing there frozen in place with her eyes wide, unsure where to sit or who to talk to. Emotionally, she feels anxious and insecure. One of her colleagues looks over and smiles. "Hey, Sarah, right?"
She stutters out something affirming that yes, she is indeed Sarah.

"Welcome!" the colleague says. "I don't know if Jerry prepped you for this, but this is a multidisciplinary team meeting, and we like to sit with people we usually don't work with. People in different teams get to know each other this way."

Sarah feels a warmth spread all over her. She takes a breath in, smiles at her colleague, and starts to say, "Okay, great," when another colleague across the room calls to her in a playful tone: "Come over here. We have a spot. I need to pick your brain about something anyhow!"
Sarah smiles a bigger smile and confidently walks over to sit.

So now what happened? She neurocepted safety this time: the smile from her coworker, gaining clarity on the group norms from the top down, and the invitation from the other coworker, with that welcoming and excited vocal tone. She accurately neurocepted safety and shifted out of freeze, out of immobility, and into a mobilized safety state.

blocks.h: You notice the effects, not neuroception itself

blocks.p: Now that you understand neuroception accurately, let's take the next step and learn how to identify it.

You can probably see that neuroception is not something we directly experience. I mean the moment of neuroception itself, the biological communication from brainstem to brain and body. Instead, we can directly experience the effects of neuroception. This is a subtle but important difference.

Sarah didn't notice the neuroception of danger before her first step landed in the conference room. She didn't even notice the effects, like shallow breathing and tense shoulders. She was too far into defensive activation. But if she had enough safety in her system, and if she was mindful enough, she would have noticed the breath and the tension. The breath and tension are the effects of neuroception, the outcome of it. These are the potentially conscious results of neuroception. We identify neuroception through its effects.

One problem with this is that neuroception affects so many different parts of you. When you shift into defense, it affects your thoughts, your emotions, your sensations, your impulses, and your behaviors.

Another problem is that you may have little to no connection with yourself. Everything from the neck down might be a stranger to you. So we need to start much smaller. We don't have to notice everything.
Here are three questions to ask yourself to identify neuroception. Write these down. You're going to be using them a lot.

ol: How is my breathing? Is it more or less shallow? Is it in my chest or my belly? Are my shoulders moving? Is it comfortable or not?
How is my muscle tension? Am I tense or relaxed? Where do I feel tension or relaxation? Is it all over, or in a specific spot?
Am I more or less likely to smile? This one is pretty straightforward. And if you are more likely to smile, then do so. Let yourself smile.

blocks.p: These are the three key areas where you look for the effects of neuroception.

blocks.h: The practice: one sense, on purpose

blocks.p: Let's get a little more specific, because it's time to take your first steps. You're going to look for the effects of neuroception in these three areas in response to sensory inputs in particular. When you notice, come from as much curiosity as you can, not evaluation. This isn't about good or bad, right or wrong. It's just noticing what is, what's truthful about your experience.
And you're going to do it proactively. For now, don't wait for your senses to pick something up and your body to shift, and then notice it. That's reactive. I want you to be proactive.

ol: Choose an experience that engages just one of your senses. Not all of them, just one. Mindfully experience the taste, sight, feel, smell, or sound of something.
Take in the sensory input, then ask the three questions. Notice how it impacts your breathing, your muscle tension, and whether you're more or less likely to smile.

blocks.p: How do you do this? I bet you have a candle in your home. Smell it mindfully and ask yourself those three questions. Next time you're at Target or Walmart or some other store, go to the candle aisle and smell one of the candles there. You're probably going to have a coffee at some point. Taste it, and answer those three questions. Real easy. These are things you would do anyway.

Focus on proactively experiencing the effects of neuroception. As this becomes easier, then notice how your body reacts to sensory inputs you don't expect. If you can't catch it in the moment, the way Sarah didn't in the story, reflect back on those moments at the end of the day.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: You might be wondering why this is important and how it helps, especially because you want to get unstuck. Noticing the effects of neuroception builds self-awareness without judgment. That's huge. If you're going to continue down the unstuck path, this is a huge component of it.

Further down the unstucking road, you'll need to build your ability to notice how your body is, what it wants, and how it reacts. The self-awareness you build now tells you what cues safety and what cues defense. Later, you'll learn what cues safety in your body, but you need to feel it. You'll also learn how to mindfully access and feel defensive activation, and again, that requires a lot of nonjudgmental connection with yourself. You're not there yet. If you've just learned the Polyvagal Theory and you're trying to put things into place, those pieces are further down the road. But as you progress, they'll become way more important.

Over time, as you become more comfortable noticing how your body responds, you'll begin to understand what it wants. Our bodies are compelled to self-regulate, to get unstuck from defense and access more safety. But to get there, we need to consciously listen to what our body needs.

When it needs to squeeze to release stuck fight activation, we need to listen and act on it. When it needs to hug another and receive warmth and comfort, we need to listen to it. When it needs to collapse face first on the bed and breathe in silence, recovering from the day, we need to listen to it.

This simple, proactive sensory practice with the three questions is a small step in that direction. Small but sustainable, and small but significant, especially if you're just starting. It's also useful because it puts you in the driver's seat. You decide what sensory input you use and when, and you decide to look inward and notice your body's reaction.

I'll bet you typically live reactively. You react to things. You react to the state of your body. You try to numb what it's going through, or distract yourself. What I'm suggesting is the opposite. It's proactive, and it helps you connect, not numb or distract, but directly connect with your body in the present moment.
So here's your next step: proactively connect with one sense, and notice how your body responds to what it neurocepts. You got this.
